summary:
Maluku stands under Indonesia's national framework. Both audited sources for this province are national in scope and neither records a Maluku-specific ordinance, enforcement action, protection scheme or service, so the assessment below rests on the national picture those sources document.

The penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual sexual activity between adults outside marriage. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records a maximum of two years' imprisonment, while the national overview notes a term of up to one year where an immediate family member lodges the complaint. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, every sexual act by a same-sex couple falls within the outside-marriage offence, and reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Criminalisation below the national level is concentrated in Aceh, where Sharia-based penalties reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors: two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship there in February 2025. The Human Dignity Trust profile also lists South Sumatra as criminalising same-sex conduct between men and between women. Neither province is Maluku, and the national overview identifies Aceh as the outlier rather than any eastern province.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

One death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody is directly documented. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. The Diplomat reported in August 2026 that the government is codifying anti-LGBT provisions while vigilante mobs attack transgender women, and commentators quoted by ABC News stated that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Legal gender recognition is available only after sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval, and only the sex descriptors 'male' and 'female' are recognised, with no third-gender option or X marker on Indonesian documents. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing electronic ID cards to transgender Indonesians, operating in nine provinces.

National law provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection on the grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the Constitution is silent on both. On 14 December 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected a petition to criminalise homosexuality by five votes to four.
tangentialFactors:
Social climate bears on street-level risk for a trans visitor. A 2023 Pew Research survey found that 95% of Indonesians oppose same-sex marriage, and Indonesia voted against the establishment of the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity.

The sub-national picture is uneven rather than uniform: Aceh applies religious criminal penalties that other provinces do not, and the Human Dignity Trust profile records South Sumatra as a second province with its own same-sex criminalisation provisions. A visitor's exposure therefore changes at provincial boundaries, though neither of the audited sources addresses that variation for Maluku.
localsOnly:
Residents of Maluku hold no recognised relationship status with a same-sex partner, and the outside-marriage provisions of the penal code that took effect on 2 January 2026 apply to them on the same terms as elsewhere in Indonesia, with a family-complaint route that the national overview records as carrying up to one year's imprisonment.

Change of legal gender requires sex-reassignment surgery followed by court approval, and documents carry only 'male' or 'female'. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has issued electronic ID cards to transgender Indonesians through an outreach programme running in nine provinces.

Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination or bias-motivated violence, and no hate-crime provision covers conduct motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity. The Constitutional Court's 5-4 refusal on 14 December 2017 to criminalise homosexuality means the criminal exposure residents face runs through the outside-marriage articles and, for those in Aceh, through provincial religious law.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records any Maluku-specific ordinance, provincial regulation, police practice, hate-crime incident, shelter, clinic or service. The absence of such records is a gap in the retrieved material, not a finding that none exist; the Wikipedia page for the province returned no usable finding.

Whether Maluku is one of the nine provinces covered by the Ministry of Home Affairs ID-card outreach is not sourced and remains unresolved here, as is any data on access to gender-affirming care, facilities, or documentation services within the province.

Retrieval limits affect two sources. The 2022 wire report on police denying mistreatment in the death in custody of a transgender activist was not retrievable and is relied on through a fetch-time summary, and the August 2026 feature was available only through navigation, headline and dossier summary at fetch.
